To apply the ratio test we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{{x}^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{3/2}}\cdot \frac{{n}^{3/2}}{{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{n}{n+1})}^{3/2}|x| \\  & =|x|{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{n}{n+1})}^{3/2} \\  & =|x|\cdot 1 \\  & =|x|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for $|x|<1.$ So, the radius of convergence is $1,$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-1,1).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x|=1,$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=-1$ and $x=1$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{1}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{2}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{3}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{4}^{3/2}}+⋯\,,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the $p$-series test.  So the endpoint $x=1$ is included in our interval.

- When $x=-1$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3/2}} \\  & =-\,\frac{1}{{1}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{2}^{3/2}}-\frac{1}{{3}^{3/2}}+\frac{1}{{4}^{3/2}}+⋯\,,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test.  So the endpoint $x=-1$ is included in our interval.

Therefore, the interval of convergence is $[-1,1].$
